A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same COMPASS study. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: V1 reports original segmentation experiments on four datasets, including interval lengths, empirical coverage, distribution-shift experiments, and supplementary SegResNet results.

after.justification: V2 retains original segmentation experiments and adds empirical analyses of feature layers, PCA components, calibration stability, and computational runtime.

M1.justification: V1 constructs intervals from two perturbed endpoints and assumes nestedness. V2 introduces minimum/maximum envelopes over the perturbation range, with a sweep-based procedure for non-monotonic responses and corresponding asymmetric envelopes. This substantially extends the proposed procedure, although the PCA directions remain unchanged and reported experiments still use endpoint evaluation.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate segmentation area on EBHI, HAM10000, TN3K, and Kvasir, including distribution shifts on H&E and skin lesions. The new analyses examine retained data and tasks; revised class allocations and model configurations do not establish new coverage.

E2.justification: V2 removes FCP from the empirical coverage comparison in Table 2, while retaining its conceptual oracle interval-length comparison in Table 3. SCP, Output-CQR, Local CP, and E2E-CQR remain the other evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Section 3.2 changes stated calibration/test allocations from 60/40 to 40/60 for H&E adenocarcinoma and from 70/30 to 30/70 for skin-lesion nevi, and revises the training-partition description. New analyses introduce five ground-truth bins, 1–5 PCA components, and layer/aggregation comparisons. V2 Figure 6 retains the old allocations, so the PDFs establish reported protocol revisions without establishing that the shift experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds layer-choice ablations, PCA-component sensitivity, spatially aggregated versus flattened Jacobian analyses, calibration performance across ground-truth bins, and runtime analyses (Table 4, Table 8, Figures 5 and 7–11). The original perturbation trajectories and segmentation examples are retained, not newly added.

E5.justification: Both versions report 100 randomized calibration/test splits, mean±standard-deviation results, and 95% confidence intervals. The added analyses extend these reporting conventions without stating a changed uncertainty-estimation procedure, increased repeat count for retained experiments, or new significance testing.

E6.justification: U-Net results change throughout Tables 1–2. For H&E at alpha=0.10, COMPASS-J interval length changes from 2512±160 to 3160±336 pixels squared and coverage from 0.895±0.029 to 0.907±0.029; COMPASS-L becomes the shortest-interval method. V2 also adds ablation, conditional-coverage, and runtime findings and removes FCP coverage entries. Weighted and SegResNet table values remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Theorem 1 and Appendix A replace assumed nestedness with a minimum/maximum envelope construction and a nestedness proof. Theorem 3 and Appendix B similarly redefine asymmetric bounds using one-sided envelopes and revise the proofs. The main theorem also relaxes the stated metric requirement from differentiable to measurable.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction strengthen the central coverage claim from requiring exchangeability and nestedness to requiring exchangeability, with nestedness supplied by the new construction. Claims about efficient medical segmentation intervals and correction under covariate shift otherwise remain substantially unchanged.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive explanations linking Jacobian variance to gradient alignment and monotonicity, and spatial aggregation to reduced dependence on object position. It explains COMPASS-L adaptivity, recommends layer/component choices and an envelope fallback, and discusses sparse-bin undercoverage. Section 3.2 also shifts its interpretation toward deep-feature weighting as essential for robustness.

D1.justification: Code changes from a promised release upon acceptance to reported availability. V2 additionally documents sigmoid-summed area computation, Jacobian precomputation, and timing hardware, feature dimensions, and calibration sample counts. Most architecture, optimizer, preprocessing, and baseline hyperparameter details are retained.

R1.justification: V2 adds Belhasin et al. and explicitly connects COMPASS to principal-direction uncertainty sets. It also replaces the Davenport citation with Mossina and Friedrich's morphological prediction-set work. The broader positioning relative to output-space CP and FCP remains stable.

P1.justification: Coverage and calibration explanations and Appendices A–C are substantially rewritten. Appendix C is reorganized into training, verification, and calibration/inference stages; the standalone conclusion is removed; practical considerations and disclosure statements are added. Citation style also changes from numbered references to author–year.

P2.justification: V2 adds six analytical figures and two tables, extensively reformats existing tables, revises captions, and reorganizes algorithm displays and appendix layout. The original workflow image, score-compression plot, perturbation trajectories, and segmentation overlays are retained despite relocation or renumbering.

improvement.justification: The clearer envelope/endpoint distinction, new layer/PCA and calibration diagnostics, runtime evidence, and reported code availability make v2 more useful and its implementation choices easier to assess. These gains are tempered by conflicting shift allocations in Section 3.2 and Figure 6, unchanged weighted results despite revised protocol descriptions, and removal of FCP coverage results. The net improvement is useful but limited by these unresolved reporting inconsistencies.
